query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Processing the Ti–Ni–based high-entropy alloy under ultra‐high purity, oxygen‐ and nitrogen‐free conditions (e.g., by vacuum arc remelting with in situ degassing or using getters) will minimize the formation of deleterious interstitial-induced precipitates and phase segregation, thereby enhancing its elevated-temperature strength and ductility compared to an identically composed alloy produced under standard (ambient‐contaminant) conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy whose main constituents are titanium and nickel (with the remaining principal elements chosen to yield a homogeneous phase) produced by conventional melting methods that result in typical interstitial impurity levels.
generation.intervention: Adopt a processing route that strictly minimizes oxygen and nitrogen contamination—such as vacuum arc remelting under ultra-high-purity inert atmosphere with in situ degassing or the use of oxygen/nitrogen getters—to achieve greatly reduced interstitial impurity levels.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., compressive or tensile tests at 1000–1400 °C) conducted in an inert or vacuum environment, comparing samples processed under standard versus ultra-high purity conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The reduced presence of interstitial impurities (O and N) will suppress the nucleation of deleterious secondary phases (e.g., brittle α-Ti or oxide precipitates) that can form at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: By lowering the impurity content, the uniform single-phase solid solution is maintained at elevated temperatures, so the beneficial solid solution strengthening is unimpeded by precipitate-induced softening or embrittlement. This cleaner matrix is more effective in sustaining a higher yield strength and ductility at extreme temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ultra-high-purity processed alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in elevated-temperature yield strength and improved ductility (or delayed onset of softening) relative to the same alloy produced by conventional processing.
generation.baseline: The alloy fabricated via standard arc melting in less-controlled atmospheres, containing typical interstitial levels that promote nanoscale phase segregation and softening at high temperature.
generation.boundary: This intervention hypothesis applies to titanium- and nickel-containing single-phase HEAs intended for high-temperature (1000–1400 °C) or extreme-environment structural applications. It assumes that the alloy’s composition is otherwise optimized for a homogeneous solid solution and that mechanical testing is performed in a controlled inert or vacuum environment.
generation.uncertainty: While impurity control is known to affect high-temperature behavior in related refractory alloys, the precise quantitative improvement in mechanical performance (e.g., % increase in yield strength) remains uncertain and may depend on the alloy’s exact composition and processing details.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples of the same Ti–Ni-based high-entropy alloy: one group processed through standard arc melting (control) and another processed with a vacuum arc remelting protocol designed to minimize O and N contamination. Ensure all other processing parameters (composition, cooling rate, etc.) are equal. Subject both groups to identical elevated-temperature mechanical tests.
measurements: Quantification of interstitial oxygen and nitrogen levels (e.g., via inert gas fusion analysis)
Phase identification and microstructural analysis (XRD, TEM) before and after exposure to high temperature
Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures (yield strength, ductility, work-hardening behavior)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and ductility (or delay in softening) is observed in the ultra-high-purity processed samples compared to the control group, then the hypothesis that impurity reduction via the proposed intervention improves high-temperature mechanical properties is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.
